tagline: Wooded river country holds the roadbed of the old Wally railway.
intro: Wally Road Scenic Byway belongs to Mohican River country, a landscape of wooded hilltops, deep ravines, wetlands and valley bottomlands. Ohio’s byway description emphasizes those landforms, while its byways brochure highlights woodlands and waterways.

The corridor’s railroad history survives in the roadbed of the Toledo, Walhonding Valley and Ohio railway, known as the Wally. Loudonville also drew railroad visitors: the Pennsylvania Railroad offered special fares and excursions for the town’s street fair. Canoe liveries along the Mohican now account for Loudonville’s nickname, the Canoe Capital of Ohio.

Begin in Loudonville on the Black Fork. About two miles southwest of town, the Black Fork and Clear Fork meet to form the Mohican. The river continues generally south-southeast through Holmes and Knox counties. Finish this journey at Greer, the Knox County community formerly called Greersville.

moments.title: Loudonville
moments.text: Canoes are only part of Loudonville’s transportation story. From 1913 to 1996, the village was home to the Flxible Company, which manufactured motorcycle sidecars, commercial cars and buses. During World War II, the company interrupted normal production to make war goods. A portion of the former plant later served as a parts depot and service point for Motor Coach Industries until that operation ended in December 2014. Canoe liveries along the Mohican account for the village’s Canoe Capital of Ohio nickname. The river remains another route through town: Loudonville stands on the Black Fork, within a river system navigable by canoe.

moments.title: Black Fork and Clear Fork
moments.text: The Mohican begins with two rivers meeting about two miles southwest of Loudonville. The Black Fork arrives after passing Perrysville and Loudonville; the Clear Fork comes through Mohican State Park. Together they form a river that flows generally south-southeast through Holmes and Knox counties. Farther downstream, the Mohican meets the Kokosing to form the Walhonding, another change of name in the same connected drainage.

moments.title: Greer
moments.text: Greer began as Greersville, laid out in 1836 by Robert Greer and named for him. The post office opened under that longer name in 1851. It became Greer in 1908, then closed in 1949. The community remains unincorporated, in Knox County.
